extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, and legal practitioners applying or advising under the Patents, Designs, and Trade Marks Act 1883
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal guidance on making, prosecuting, amending, and enforcing patent (and related designs/trade mark) applications under the Patents, Designs, and Trade Marks Act 1883. Covers who may apply, procedural steps, examiner/Comptroller roles, fees, amendment rules, and related provisions for designs and trade marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply for a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person (a), whether a British subject, may make an application for a patent. Two or more persons may make a joint application, and a patent may be granted to them jointly. The personal representative of an inventor who dies before applying or after application but before grant may obtain the patent. A body corporate may apply. The application must be made in the English language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text (s.4): joint applications permitted; married women, infants, etc., may apply; corporate applicants will be registered by corporate name (Patents Rules, 70).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must be the first and true inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The person applying must, in order to obtain a valid patent, be the first and true inventor of an invention within the meaning of sect. 6 of the Statute of Monopolies; otherwise the patent, if granted, will be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See definitions of 'Patent' and 'Invention' in sect. 46.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application form and signature formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining the application form (obtainable on payment of £1), the applicant is required to sign it himself. The signature, since it contains a declaration, ought to be made before an officer duly authorised to administer declarations (commissioner or notary). If signed before a Justice of the Peace no extra stamp will be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tip: signatures before JPs avoid delay for extra stamps (Law Times citation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of provisional specification recommended
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the application may be accompanied by the complete specification, inventors are advised to send merely a provisional specification to gain time to perfect their inventions and to avoid the risk of losing the £3 paid for the complete specification if the application is refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional protection commonly used; majority of applications use provisional specifications (see tabular comparison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and duty of Examiner (examination not conclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Examiner is appointed to report on whether the invention is the proper subject-matter for a patent. His duties are restricted to ascertaining if the invention is fairly described, if the application is properly prepared, and if the title sufficiently indicates the subject-matter. The acceptance of the application is not conclusive as to the sufficiency of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination is to assist applicants in framing specifications but does not relieve the legal duty to sufficiently describe an invention. Sect. 5(4) requires more (ascertain nature and manner of performance and drawings if required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete specification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: By sect. 5, sub-sect. (4), the complete specification must not merely 'particularly describe the nature of the invention' but must also 'ascertain the nature of the invention, and in what manner it is to be performed, and must be accompanied by drawings, if required.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recital on sealed patent does not itself satisfy all statutory requirements for the complete specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller may require amendment; appeals to Law Officer
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comptroller may require the application to be amended, subject to an appeal to the law officer. Requests for amendment are advertised and any person may oppose. If leave to amend is refused, the applicant may appeal to the law officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See p.10; appeals to law officers may be numerous and their workload is a practical concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of specification (timing and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification may be amended before sealing, after sealing, or even during action. The leave of the Comptroller must be obtained in each case, and where an action is pending, the permission of the Court is required to apply for such leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In no case is an amendment to be allowed which would make the amended specification claim an invention substantially different from that in the original specification; leave to amend is conclusive as to the right to amend (sect. 18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment during action — limitation on damages recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: If amendment is allowed during an action, patentees cannot recover damages in the action unless they satisfy the court that the claim was framed in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical limitation reduces opportunistic broadening of claims during litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and their treatment for pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate whether fees for applications made before 31 Dec. 1883 are governed by old law or by the Act. The text argues that once a patent is granted, provisions of the Act apply and fees may be paid by instalments; the Patent Office takes a different view (requiring the 7th year's £100 lump sum for pre-1884 applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office Instructions (17) and suggested remedy: Board of Trade to issue new letters patent forms under sect. 101 to avoid difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction and timing of patent payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the new Act a patent will be obtainable for £4 initially, with the £50 payment postponed from the 3rd to the 4th year; the later payments remain unaltered. The Act reduces the number of office calls and documents and alters timing of payments (schedules of fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical comparison shows simplification from many calls/payments to only two calls and two payments (and ability to transact by post).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of patent to one invention (statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation of patent to one invention made statutory, with a proviso that it shall not be competent in an action or other proceeding to object to a patent on the ground that it comprises more than one invention (sect. 33).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory rule both narrows claims and prevents certain procedural attacks in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of provisional protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension of provisional protection from six to fifteen months, or from application to sealing of patent (sect. 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional protection thus covers a longer development period before sealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term and duration changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension of first term of a patent from three to four years; the total duration of patents continues to be 14 years (sect. 17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect on fees/timing noted above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit of complete specification before grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete specification must be deposited before the grant of the patent and within nine months from date of application (sect. 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures that the detailed disclosure is filed early in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment and functions of Comptroller and Examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment of Comptroller General and of Examiners to examine applications (a) to see that the application is properly prepared and that nature of invention is fairly described, (b) to compare complete specifications with provisional ones (sects. 9, 83).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners assist in form and comparison but do not determine legal sufficiency beyond stated limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal from Comptroller to Law Officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal from Comptroller to the Law Officer is provided (sects. 7, 9, 18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals procedures may affect timing and certainty of prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of prior applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Various provisions protect prior applicants (sects. 7, 10, 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sections are intended to secure rights of earlier applicants in contested priority situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent sealing and register entry
rubrics_metrics.description: On the sealing of the patent, the name of the patentee will be entered in the register. A patent is to be sealed with the seal of the Patent Office (sect. 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After sealing, persons acquiring rights (licence, mortgage, assignment) ought to register documents at once because the registered proprietor has powers subject to rights appearing on the register (sect. 87).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration (and effect) of subsequent dealings
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons who obtain subsequently any rights in the patent, by way of licence or mortgage or under any agreement, ought at once to register the document in question, since by sect. 87 the registered proprietor has, subject to any rights appearing from the register and existing equities, power absolutely to assign, grant licences as to, or otherwise deal with the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to register may affect visible title; position of unregistered assignee suing is unclear under the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty as to unregistered assignees' right to sue
rubrics_metrics.description: Under prior law an unregistered assignee could not bring an action for infringement; the wording of sect. 87 in the present Act differs and it would seem that registration is no longer necessary as a condition to an assignee suing, though the point is not clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical caution: register assignments to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal procedure simplifications (infringement and revocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action for infringement is to be tried without a jury unless otherwise ordered, and either party may call in an assessor. The certificate of validity may be obtained after trial. Revocation takes place by petition to the High Court (sect. 26) and scire facias is abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendor protection: in actions where patentee threatens proceedings against purchasers of alleged infringing articles, the vendor is not required to establish mala fides on the part of the patentee (sect. 32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for extension of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles on which the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council are to act in considering applications for extension are set out (sect. 25); extension up to 14 years may be granted in 'exceptional cases', and the committee may impose restrictions, conditions and provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial Committee should have regard to the profits of the patentee 'as such, and not as manufacturer'; no fixed guidance on amount of remuneration — wide discretion remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to grant compulsory licences
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of the Board of Trade to compel grant of licences (sect. 22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory mechanism for compulsory licensing in the Act (referenced in transitionary clauses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of clerical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerical errors in or in connection with an application may be amended by the Comptroller on payment of a nominal fee (sect. 99). There appears to be an oversight with no express provision for correction of clerical errors in the letters patent themselves after sealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 18 and sect. 91 may not apply after sealing; Board of Trade may issue new forms under sect. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs: abolish useful/ornamental distinction; novelty required
rubrics_metrics.description: The old distinction between useful and ornamental designs is abolished and any novel design, whether applicable for pattern, shape, configuration or for ornament, is entitled to registration. Registration of designs for sculpture is abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional registration is abolished; applicants are required to leave one sketch at application but must supply three exact drawings or specimens before certificate is issued and before sale/delivery of goods bearing the design (sect. 51).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design registration term
rubrics_metrics.description: For the old varying term of registration, one uniform term of four years has been substituted for all designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs Instructions referenced; practical effect is standardization of term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design assignment formalities unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: No provision is made in the Act as to the assignment of a design; although forms (Form K) mention particulars 'e.g. by deed dated, &c.' this is insufficient to require assignment to be by deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical uncertainty: lack of explicit statutory form may leave open disputes over assignment formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade marks: extended definition and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a trade mark has been extended to include fancy words, brands, and single letters in case of old marks. Statutory permission is given to register, as an addition to a trade mark, marks common to the trade provided the right to any exclusive use of such common marks be disclaimed (sect. 74). Statutory provision also made for registration of a series of marks (sect. 66).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registers must accommodate disclaimers and series; applicants should be aware of these options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark searches recommended before applying
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying for registration of a trade mark, the intending applicant should make a search at the Trade Marks Branch of the Patent Office (or Manchester Office) to ascertain whether the proposed mark is already registered or calculated to deceive by resemblance to marks already on record (sect. 72).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee for making a search is 1d(?) for each quarter of an hour (text shows 'Is. for each quarter of an hour'); if the Comptroller is to make the search a formal request for registration (fee shown as '58.') is required (Trade Marks Instructions, 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark application and agent authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration is no longer required from the applicant, and an agent may apply on the applicant's behalf provided he is authorised to act in writing signed by the applicant (Instructions, 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitates representation by agents but requires written authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and abandonment for trade marks
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application for a trade mark is refused, an appeal lies to the Board of Trade (not the Court), though the Board may refer the matter to the Court (sect. 62). An application not completed within 12 months owing to the applicant's default is to be deemed abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures procedural finality and incentivizes diligence in prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of trade marks: Act silent on formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: No express statutory provision as to the manner in which a trade mark is to be assigned in connection with the goodwill; the Act and Rules are silent on whether assignment must be by deed, though forms suggest particulars by deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of Board of Trade's power under sect. 101 to make rules on this is doubtful; practitioners should take care to document assignments clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheffield marks: change in procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of an application for registration of an assigned Sheffield mark is now given to the Comptroller by the Cutlers' Company, instead of notice of an application for assignment; the Cutlers' Company first assigns a mark and then the assignee applies to have it registered. Registration cannot take place if the Comptroller objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local/customary marks (Sheffield) have special procedural steps requiring coordination with the Cutlers' Company and the Comptroller.
